title: Uttarakhand's Butter Festival Turns an Alpine Meadow Into a Sea of Makhan
excerpt: The annual Anduri Utsav at Dayara Bugyal sees 500 villagers trek to 3,400 meters to play Holi with fresh butter and buttermilk in one of India’s most unique cultural celebrations.
body:
• Uttarakhand's Anduri Utsav, or Butter Festival, is underway at Dayara Bugyal in Uttarkashi district, with around 500 villagers climbing to the alpine meadow to play Holi with fresh butter and buttermilk.
  • The festival, held annually during Bhadon Sankranti between August 16 and 18, honors Lord Krishna as protector of cattle and expresses gratitude to Bugyal Mata, the Goddess of the Meadow.
  • Raithal village serves as the base camp for the trek to Dayara Bugyal, which sits at roughly 3,400 meters and is one of Uttarakhand's most stunning high-altitude grasslands.
  • The celebration combines pastoral tradition with cultural performances, including children staging elaborate skits of Lord Krishna's childhood, set against a backdrop of Himalayan peaks.

High in the alpine meadows of Uttarakhand, villagers are smearing fresh butter on each other's faces, drenching themselves in buttermilk and dancing to the rhythmic beats of the Dhol-Damau. The Anduri Utsav — widely known as the Butter Festival or Makhan Holi — is underway at Dayara Bugyal, one of India's most spectacular high-altitude grasslands.

The festival, held annually between August 16 and 18 during Bhadon Sankranti, is rooted in a pastoral tradition that predates living memory. Around 500 villagers from Raithal and surrounding hamlets in Uttarkashi district trek uphill to the meadow, which sits at roughly 3,400 meters above sea level, to celebrate the safe return of their cattle from summer grazing.

A Festival Born From Gratitude

The Butter Festival is dedicated to Lord Krishna in his childhood "makhan-chor" (butter thief) form. In local legend, Krishna is considered the protector of cattle grazing in the green fields of Dayara Bugyal. The celebration is an expression of gratitude both to Krishna and to Bugyal Mata, the Goddess of the Meadow, for keeping livestock safe through the grazing season.

The tradition has evolved over generations. Villagers once smeared cow dung on visiting guests as a playful greeting. That practice has given way to the more photogenic — and aromatic — custom of smearing fresh butter on faces while pouring buttermilk over one another, turning the meadow into a sea of white.

The Trek to Dayara Bugyal

Reaching the festival requires a trek from Raithal village, located about 38 km from Uttarkashi town. The village itself is a charming settlement known for traditional stone-and-wood architecture, prosperous agriculture and goat breeding. The trek from Raithal to the bugyal (meadow) passes through dense forests of oak and rhododendron before opening onto sweeping grasslands framed by snow-capped Himalayan peaks.

Raithal is roughly 11 hours by road from Delhi via NH334 and NH34, making it accessible for a long weekend trip. The nearest airport is Jolly Grant in Dehradun, and Uttarkashi serves as the nearest major transit point with hotel and homestay options.

More Than Butter

The festivities extend well beyond the butter-smearing. Local children stage elaborate cultural performances, including skits depicting Lord Krishna's childhood adventures, complete with costumes and traditional choreography. The villagers sing and dance to the beats of Dhol-Damau, a traditional Pahadi musical instrument, creating a joyful atmosphere that trekkers and travelers have increasingly sought out.

The festival has gained visibility among adventure travelers and trekking communities in recent years, drawing visitors who combine the cultural experience with the popular Dayara Bugyal trek. The meadow itself is one of Uttarakhand's most Instagram-worthy landscapes, a vast expanse of green rolling grassland set against a panorama of Bandarpoonch and other Himalayan peaks.

A Cultural Window for Diaspora Travelers

For members of the Indian diaspora planning trips to India, the Butter Festival offers an experience far removed from the standard temple-and-monument itinerary. It is a living cultural tradition that connects visitors to the pastoral rhythms of Himalayan life, and the late-August timing aligns with school breaks in many countries.

The trek is rated moderate difficulty, suitable for reasonably fit hikers without technical mountaineering experience. Several homestays in Raithal offer accommodation, and local guides can be arranged through Uttarakhand Tourism or independent operators.

Getting There

The most common route is by road from Delhi or Dehradun to Uttarkashi, then a local taxi to Raithal. From Raithal, the trek to Dayara Bugyal takes one to two days depending on the route chosen. The festival itself runs during Bhadon Sankranti, typically August 16 to 18, with the main celebrations on the second day when the largest procession reaches the meadow.
